content: In Sierra Leone, a pregnant woman presented in labor at a general hospital and underwent a cesarean delivery. Two days after delivery, she developed symptoms of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and subsequently died. Post-mortem testing using a buccal swab confirmed the diagnosis of EVD. Her infant developed symptoms at three days of life and died seven days later. Investigators identified 46 individuals who had contact with the woman during her time at the healthcare facility, six of whom contracted laboratory-confirmed EVD. It was revealed that nurses, hospital cleaning staff, and caregivers lacked access to recommended personal protective equipment (PPE). Additional factors contributing to the high risk of exposure included failure to recognize EVD infection, exposure to infected bodily fluids, and inadequate isolation precautions. In another case in 2014, Connolly and Young conducted contact tracing for a pregnant woman with undiagnosed Ebola Virus (EBOV) who delivered in a maternity ward. Investigators identified multiple lapses in infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, which likely contributed to EVD transmission to two maternity ward patients and their infants. One patient was delivered by the same nurse who attended the index patient, and the nurse’s PPE was both incomplete and contaminated. Furthermore, the delivery suite was not cleaned between deliveries. The second maternity patient was likely infected due to a lack of standard precautions, as she was placed next to the index case during her delivery and subsequent hemorrhage. Detectable EBOV RNA has been identified in pregnancy-related fluids and tissues, including amniotic fluid, placental tissue, fetal tissue, and vaginal secretions, even in pregnant women with mild or unrecognized disease. Viral persistence in these fluids and tissues has been documented after the virus has been cleared from the blood. For example, EBOV was isolated from fetal tissue in a woman who delivered a stillborn fetus one month after EVD exposure. Another woman in Sierra Leone delivered a stillborn fetus that tested positive for EBOV RNA, despite her blood testing negative for EBOV RNA and IgM antibodies, though she was IgG antibody positive. In reproductive tract specimens from non-pregnant individuals, EBOV RNA was detected up to 36 days following symptom onset, though menstrual blood samples tested negative. EBOV RNA has also been detected in the breast milk of women with acute and convalescent EVD up to 26 days after symptom onset, as well as in asymptomatic women. Two lactating women were evaluated after their infants died from laboratory-confirmed EVD, and EBOV RNA was detected in their breast milk despite negative blood tests. Among 25 infants breastfed by mothers with EVD, 68% developed presumed or laboratory-confirmed EVD, with a mortality rate of 82%. However, eight infants breastfed by EVD-positive women did not become ill. Breastfeeding alone was not identified as a risk factor for EVD transmission. The rVSV-ZEBOV-GP Ebola vaccine (Ervebo) is recommended for pregnant and breastfeeding women during active Zaire EBOV outbreaks, provided it is administered under rigorous research protocols or compassionate use guidelines with informed consent. The vaccine has demonstrated very good efficacy in the general population, though no studies have determined its efficacy specifically in pregnant women. In a 2015 trial, 43 vaccinated women became pregnant, but no laboratory-confirmed EVD cases occurred among participants, preventing efficacy assessment in this subgroup. Data from other studies suggest that pregnancy outcomes among vaccinated women are comparable to those of unvaccinated women. Management of pregnant women with suspected or confirmed EVD requires specialized care. Overlap in symptoms between early EVD and pregnancy-related conditions necessitates evaluation by obstetric and Ebola-response-trained healthcare providers. Pregnant women should be treated in designated spaces within Ebola Treatment Centers (ETCs) with measures to ensure privacy. Obstetric complications should be managed on a case-by-case basis, prioritizing maternal indications and considering resource availability. Surgical procedures should be performed only by experienced personnel using full PPE, with decontamination of the site afterward. Induced abortion or labor induction may be considered for women with acute EVD or following recovery. Comprehensive counseling on pregnancy risks and management options should be provided. Products of conception should be treated as potentially infectious, and Ebola-specific PPE must be used during procedures. Labor induction or abortion should occur in private areas within ETCs, and psychosocial support should be offered due to the poor pregnancy outcomes associated with EVD. For EVD survivors with ongoing pregnancies, close monitoring and frequent antenatal care (ANC) visits are essential. Outpatient management may be an option for stable patients with reliable transportation and access to medical care. However, these women should be readmitted to ETCs for delivery to minimize the risk of EVD transmission.
